(* Next state                                                              *)
(***************************************************************************)
\* derives: F1.1 -- a protocol step: the schedule position stays, the armed trigger may fire
Sys(A) == A /\ Obs /\ UNCHANGED <<pc, ngc>>
\* derives: C1.1, C1.2, C1.3, C1.4, C2.1, C2.2, C3.1, C3.4, C3.5, C3.7, C3.8
Protocol ==
  \/ \E n \in Lease : Sys(Elect(n)) \/ Sys(TimeoutSpur(n)) \/ Sys(StepDown(n))
                      \/ Sys(Decide(n)) \/ Sys(Supersede(n))
                      \/ (role[n] = "C" /\ \E Q \in SUBSET Voters(n) : Sys(Win(n, Q)))
  \/ \E n, m \in Lease : Sys(AE(n, m)) \/ Sys(TermProp(n, m)) \/ Sys(Gossip(n, m))
  \/ \E n, m \in Lease : \E x \in rq[n] : Sys(Forward(n, m, x))
  \/ \E n, m \in Lease : Sys(FwdCfg(n, m))
  \/ \E n \in Lease : \E x \in rq[n] : Sys(ProposeQ(n, x))
  \/ \E n \in Lease : \E x \in Items(n) : Sys(ProposeCfg(n, x))
  \/ \E n \in Lease : \E x \in rep[n] : Sys(Resend(n, x))
  \/ \E m \in net : Sys(DeliverGM(m)) \/ Sys(DeliverW(m)) \/ Sys(DeliverR(m))
                    \/ Sys(DeliverWA(m)) \/ Sys(DeliverRA(m)) \/ Sys(DeliverRC(m)) \/ Sys(DeliverRCA(m))
  \/ \E o \in sout : Sys(SendOut(o))
  \/ \E c \in Clients : Sys(Retransmit(c))
\* derives: C1.1, C1.2, C1.3, C1.4, C2.1, C2.2, C3.1, C3.4, C3.5, C3.7, C3.8, F1.1, F1.2, F1.3, F2.1, F2.2, F3.1, F3.2, F3.3
Next == Take \/ Protocol
\* derives: C1.1, C1.2, C1.3, C2.1, C2.2, C3.1, C3.5, C3.7, C3.8 -- safety is checked on every behaviour
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

(***************************************************************************)
(* End of a run (Rule E1)                                                  *)
(***************************************************************************)
\* derives: C1.4, C3.4 -- quiescent: nothing in flight, nobody waiting, nothing pending at an up receiver
Quiescent ==
  /\ pc > NSteps
  /\ \A m \in net : ~(Up(Dest(m)) /\ ~(Dest(m) \in Clients /\ paused[Dest(m)]))
  /\ (alive[S] => sout = {})
  /\ \A c \in Clients : (alive[c] /\ ~paused[c]) => creq[c] = 0
  /\ \A n \in Lease : alive[n] => pend[n] = NoPend
\* derives: C1.4, C3.4
EndReached == pc > NSteps /\ IF EndT.kind = "quiescent" THEN Quiescent ELSE fired
\* derives: C1.4, C3.4 -- violated exactly when a run reaches its end (used to export a witness trace)
NotEnded == ~EndReached

(***************************************************************************)
(* Safety invariants (checked on every state of every behaviour)           *)
(***************************************************************************)
\* derives: C1.1 -- (a) no two grants carry one token; (b) a higher epoch carries a higher token
C1_1_Tokens ==
  /\ \A g, h \in gr : g # h => g.tok # h.tok
  /\ \A g, h \in gr : g.ep < h.ep => g.tok < h.tok
\* derives: C1.1 -- (c) in every log, decided grants appear in increasing token order (a node agrees in log order)
C1_1_AgreeOrder ==
  \A n \in Lease : \A i, j \in 1..Len(log[n]) :
     (i < j /\ log[n][i].k = "g" /\ log[n][j].k = "g"
      /\ (\E r \in gr : r.tok = log[n][i].tok /\ r.term = log[n][i].t)
      /\ (\E r \in gr : r.tok = log[n][j].tok /\ r.term = log[n][j].t)) => log[n][i].tok < log[n][j].tok
\* derives: C1.1 -- grants carrying one term were decided by one incarnation of one node; one leader per term
C1_1_Terms ==
  /\ \A g, h \in gr : g.term = h.term => (g.d = h.d /\ g.di = h.di)
  /\ \A a, b \in Lease : (a # b /\ role[a] = "L" /\ role[b] = "L") => term[a] # term[b]
\* derives: C1.2 -- storage accepts a write only if its token is at least the highest token storage has ever
\* accepted (hiw, before the step), and the ledger then records it; it rejects only below the ledger
C1_2(h) == \A k \in 1..Len(ev) :
          /\ ev[k].event = "WriteAccept" => (ev[k].token >= ev[k].highest_before /\ ev[k].token >= h
                                             /\ ledger = ev[k].token)
          /\ ev[k].event = "WriteReject" => (ev[k].token < ev[k].highest_before /\ ledger = ev[k].highest_before)
\* derives: C1.3 -- a client is told success only for a write storage accepted
C1_3 == \A k \in 1..Len(ev) : (ev[k].event = "WriteAck" /\ ev[k].outcome = "accepted") => ev[k].wid \in acc
\* derives: C2.1 -- storage serves a read only if its token is at least the highest token ever accepted (hiw,
\* before the step); serving does not move the ledger
C2_1(h) == \A k \in 1..Len(ev) :
          /\ ev[k].event = "ReadAccept" => (ev[k].token >= ev[k].highest_before /\ ev[k].token >= h
                                            /\ ledger = ev[k].highest_before)
          /\ ev[k].event = "ReadReject" => ev[k].token < ev[k].highest_before
\* derives: C2.2 -- a client is given only a value storage served for that read
C2_2 == \A k \in 1..Len(ev) :
          (ev[k].event = "ReadAck" /\ ev[k].outcome = "served") => [id |-> ev[k].xid, val |-> ev[k].value] \in srv
\* derives: C3.1 -- at most one configuration per epoch; e+1 only after e
C3_1 == /\ \A a, b \in dc : a.ep = b.ep => a = b
        /\ \A a \in dc : a.ep > 0 => \E b \in dc : b.ep = a.ep - 1
\* derives: C3.7 -- a grant: its decider's current configuration, recorded, counted by an eligible majority of it
C3_7 == \A k \in 1..Len(ev) : ev[k].event = "Grant" =>
          LET g == ev[k] IN
          /\ g.inputs.config_epoch = g.config_epoch
          /\ g.config_epoch = Cur(g.proc)
          /\ \E x \in dc : x.ep = g.config_epoch /\ x.mem = g.inputs.members
          /\ 2 * Cardinality({p[1] : p \in {y \in g.inputs.agreed : GElig(y[1], y[2], g.config_epoch)}})
               > Cardinality(GMem(g.config_epoch))
\* derives: C3.8 -- a commit: eligible majorities of e and of e+1, members those of its request; success told only after it
C3_8 == \A k \in 1..Len(ev) :
          /\ (ev[k].event = "ConfigCommitted" /\ ev[k].decided) =>
               LET c == ev[k]
                   e == c.epoch - 1
                   P == c.inputs.agreed
               IN /\ \E x \in dc : x.ep = e /\ x.mem = c.inputs.old_members
                  /\ 2 * Cardinality({p[1] : p \in {y \in P : GElig(y[1], y[2], e)}}) > Cardinality(GMem(e))
                  /\ 2 * Cardinality({p[1] : p \in {y \in P : y[1] \in c.members /\ (y[2] = 0 \/ y \in GReadm(e))}})
                       > Cardinality(c.members)
                  /\ \E r \in rqs : r.rid = c.request_id /\ r.mem = c.members
          /\ (ev[k].event = "ReconfigAck" /\ ev[k].outcome = "committed") =>
               \E x \in dc : x.rid = ev[k].request_id /\ x.ep = ev[k].epoch
\* derives: C3.5 -- every decision is the fixed function of its recorded inputs
C3_5 == \A k \in 1..Len(ev) :
          LET e == ev[k] IN
          /\ e.event \in {"WriteAccept", "WriteReject"} =>
               /\ (e.event = "WriteAccept") = (e.inputs.token >= e.inputs.ledger)
               /\ e.token = e.inputs.token /\ e.highest_before = e.inputs.ledger
          /\ e.event \in {"ReadAccept", "ReadReject"} =>
               /\ (e.event = "ReadAccept") = (e.inputs.token >= e.inputs.ledger)
               /\ e.token = e.inputs.token /\ e.highest_before = e.inputs.ledger
               /\ e.event = "ReadAccept" => e.value = e.inputs.stored_value
          /\ e.event = "Grant" =>
               /\ e.config_epoch = e.inputs.config_epoch /\ e.grantor_term = e.inputs.grantor_term
          /\ (e.event = "ConfigCommitted" /\ e.decided) =>
               /\ e.epoch = e.inputs.old_epoch + 1 /\ e.members = e.inputs.requested_members
               /\ e.readmits = {p \in e.inputs.agreed : p[2] > 0 /\ p[1] \in e.members}

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Reach table: for every schedule run, what the schedule needs the model to reach and the bounds it ran at.

derives: C1.1, C1.4, C3.1, C3.4, F1.1, F1.2, F1.3, F2.1, F2.2, F3.1, F3.2, F3.3
(the brief's "Reach" rule: a PASS from a space that cannot contain what the schedule needs is not a PASS)

usage: reach.py [results-dir]   prints a Markdown table from results/schedules/*/result.json and the observe traces
"""
import glob
import json
import os
import sys

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))


def witness_facts(path):
    """derives: C1.1, C3.1, F3.3 -- what the exported witness actually reached"""
    toks, terms, epochs, amn, restarts = set(), set(), set(), 0, 0
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        return None
    for ln in open(path):
        r = json.loads(ln)
        if r['event'] == 'Grant':
            toks.add(r['token'])
            terms.add(r['grantor_term'])
        if r['event'] == 'ConfigCommitted' and r.get('decided'):
            epochs.add(r['epoch'])
        if r['event'] == 'Fault' and r.get('amnesia'):
            amn += 1
        elif r['event'] == 'Fault' and 'restart' in r:
            restarts += 1
    return {'tokens': max(toks) if toks else 0, 'grants': len(toks), 'max_term': max(terms) if terms else 0,
            'epochs': max(epochs) if epochs else 0, 'amnesic': amn, 'restarts': restarts}


def main(argv):
    base = argv[0] if argv else os.path.join(HERE, 'results', 'schedules')
    rows = []
    for d in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(base, '*')), key=lambda p: (len(os.path.basename(p)), p)):
        f = os.path.join(d, 'result.json')
        if not os.path.exists(f):
            continue
        r = json.load(open(f))
        m = r.get('meta', {})
        w = witness_facts(os.path.join(d, 'witness.jsonl')) or witness_facts(os.path.join(d, 'counterexample.jsonl'))
        need = (f"epochs {m.get('reconfigs', 0)}; restarts {m.get('restarts', 0)}; amnesic {m.get('amnesic', 0)}; "
                f"clock steps {m.get('clock_steps') or '-'} ticks; grants >= {m.get('requests', 0)}; "
                f"elections >= {1 + m.get('leader_losses', 0) - (1 if m.get('reconfigs') else 0)}")
        bounds = f"MaxTerm {r.get('max_term')} (+{len(m.get('lease', []))} after last fault); spurious {r.get('spur')}"
        st = r.get('safety', {})
        reached = '-' if not w else (f"tokens to {w['tokens']}, terms to {w['max_term']}, epochs to {w['epochs']}, "
                                     f"amnesic {w['amnesic']}")
        rows.append(f"| {r['name']} | {need} | {bounds} | {st.get('distinct', '?'):,} states, depth "
                    f"{st.get('depth', '?')}, {st.get('seconds', '?')} s | {reached} | {r['verdict']} |"
                    if isinstance(st.get('distinct'), int) else
                    f"| {r['name']} | {need} | {bounds} | {st} | {reached} | {r['verdict']} |")
    print('| Schedule | Must reach | Bounds run at | Explored (safety + liveness) | Witness reached | Verdict |')
    print('|---|---|---|---|---|---|')
    print('\n'.join(rows))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    sys.exit(main(sys.argv[1:]))

input.content:
# model-regen: the TLA+ model side of tupay, built fresh from contract v3 and failure model v3

derives: C1.1, C1.2, C1.3, C1.4, C2.1, C2.2, C3.1, C3.4, C3.5, C3.7, C3.8, F1.1, F1.2, F1.3, F2.1, F2.2, F3.1, F3.2, F3.3

This directory is the model half of every pair in `tests/pairs-v4.md` (P1 to P33, P40 to P54, P58 to P63), written
from `contract/v3.md`, `failure-model/v3.md`, the schedule format (v2.2 to v5), the observability schema (v1 to v5)
and the steward's decision-replay check, and nothing else. Predictions were committed before any of it existed
(`PREDICTIONS.md`, commit `be79db9`). Results are in `RESULTS.md`; this file says what was built, how to run it, what
the model abstracts, how I read the inputs, the bounds and what they reach, and what I believe it cannot show.

## How to run

```
model-regen/run.sh P1                 # one schedule: prints PASS, FAIL <clause> or UNEXPLAINED <reason>
model-regen/run.sh --all              # every testbed/schedules/*.yaml (any name the format accepts)
model-regen/run.sh --mutations        # every pair's mutant on its pair's shared schedule
model-regen/run.sh P31 --spur 0 --max-term 3 --sims 4    # bounds and the number of random witness traces
```

Requirements: Java 21, `/opt/tlaplus/tla2tools.jar` (TLC 2.19), `uv` with `pyyaml==6.0.3` in its offline cache.
Environment: `TLC_HEAP` (default `10g`), `TLC_WORKERS` (48), `TLC_TIMEOUT` seconds per TLC run (5400),
`MODEL_SIMS` random witness traces per schedule (8). Generated TLC inputs go to `tmp/model-regen/<name>/` (never
committed); each run writes `observe/<run>.jsonl` (the counterexample if there is one, otherwise the shortest
behaviour that reaches the schedule's end) and `model-regen/results/schedules/<name>/` (verdict, TLC tails, traces,
the decision-replay report). `run.sh` resolves `testbed/schedules/<name>.yaml` and accepts any schedule in the format;
a schedule the format does not allow is reported `UNEXPLAINED rejected <reason>`.

One run of `run.sh <name>`:
1. `compile.py` turns the YAML into `MC.tla` (the schedule as TLA+ constants) and three TLC configurations.
2. TLC explores, breadth first and exhaustively within the bounds below, `SpecL` against every safety invariant
   and per-step property, and the liveness clauses in terminal form (see Liveness). A violation is `FAIL <clause>`
   with its counterexample exported; a terminal state with an unmet C1.4 or C3.4 obligation is `FAIL C1.4` or
   `FAIL C3.4`, or `UNEXPLAINED bound` if it sits at the term bound.
3. TLC finds the shortest behaviour that reaches the schedule's end (`NotEnded` as an invariant); none means
   `UNEXPLAINED end unreachable` (Rule E2: only when no violation was witnessed).
4. TLC samples `MODEL_SIMS` more behaviours to the end at random (simulation mode), for C3.5 across runs.
5. `observe/decision_replay.py` runs on every exported trace of the run; a report is `FAIL` with the clause it names
   (`C3.5` for equal inputs with unequal outcomes).

Files: `Lease.tla` (the model), `compile.py` (schedule compiler), `export.py` (TLC trace to `observe/<run>.jsonl`),
`run.py`/`run.sh` (runner), `reach.py` (the reach table), `mutations/make.py` (generates `mutations/Lease_P<n>.tla`,
one deliberate break per pair, listed in `mutations/MUTATIONS.md`), `tlc.sh` (a bare TLC launcher used while
building), `PREDICTIONS.md`, `RESULTS.md`, `results/`.

## The protocol followed

**Raft with joint consensus**: D. Ongaro and J. Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm",
USENIX ATC 2014, sections 5 (leader election, log replication, safety) and 6 (cluster membership changes by joint
consensus); with **PreVote** and **CheckQuorum** from D. Ongaro, *Consensus: Bridging Theory and Practice*, PhD
thesis, Stanford University, 2014, sections 9.6 and 6.2. The model is a Raft abstraction in the style of published
atomic-quorum specifications: an election is one step, an AppendEntries and its acknowledgement are one step
(see Abstractions).

A grant is a Raft log entry `(client, token, lifetime, config_epoch, term)`; a membership change from epoch e to
e+1 is a joint entry (C_old,new) carrying the new members and the request; leaders also append Raft's no-op on
election when they inherit an undecided change (paper, section 8).

**Amnesic restart (F3.3).** The thesis (section 3.8) says a server that loses its persistent state cannot safely
rejoin under its old identity and can be added back as a new server through a membership change; until then it
behaves as a non-voting member (section 4.2.1). That is what the model does: an amnesic restart starts incarnation
i+1 with an empty log, term 0, no vote, and only the deployment's knowledge (its name, the lease nodes, the initial
configuration). Its acknowledgements are recorded but count toward no majority, its votes and pre-votes count for
nothing, and it may not start an election, until a commit that lists it and whose decider recorded this
incarnation's agreement re-admits it (contract v3, "Re-admission"). It stays in every denominator.

**Where the protocol is adapted to the contract** (each is a reading of the contract, listed again under
Interpretations):
- *Who decides.* Contract v3 makes a commit a decision recorded once, by one node (`decided: true` exactly once per
  epoch). In Raft every leader that advances its commit index "learns" commitment, so two leaders can each believe
  they decided the same entry. The model therefore names one decider per proposal:
  - a **grant** is decided only by the leader that created its entry, from acknowledgements in its own term (Raft's
    direct commitment rule); an entry of an earlier term that a later leader commits indirectly is never decided
    and its token is dead (the client asks again);
  - a **configuration** is decided by the request's **receiver**, acting as a distinguished learner (L. Lamport,
    "Paxos Made Simple", SIGACT News 2001, section 2.3): a leader that knows the joint entry is committed (it
    counted joint majorities over an entry of its own term at or after it) hands the receiver the agreements it
    counted, possibly relayed by one node; the receiver records them as `Agreed` and decides when they form
    eligible majorities of the old and the new membership (C3.8).
- *C_new is implied.* Raft appends C_new after C_old,new commits; here a node uses the new membership alone once it
  knows epoch e+1 decided, and the joint one while the entry is in its log undecided. A leader not in the new
  membership steps down when it learns the decision.
- *Grants pause during a change.* A leader proposes no grant while a configuration entry in its log is undecided,
  and a grant is decided only under the decider's current configuration (C3.7).
- *A grant proposal carries its Raft entry term* (the contract's proposal fields plus `term`), so two entries with
  one token from different leaders are different proposals.
- *Requests reach a leader through a member.* A non-leader that receives a client's request or an operator's
  request passes it to a leader it reaches (directly, or through one member that reaches one), as Raft followers
  redirect; the receiver stays the node that records the outcome and answers the operator. A grant reply goes
  straight to the client, or back through the node that forwarded the request if the decider cannot reach the
  client (H9).

## Abstractions (what the model does not represent, and why)

- **Messages between lease nodes are atomic.** An AppendEntries and the follower's acknowledgement are one step,
  taken only while leader→follower is up; the acknowledgement is lost if follower→leader is down at that moment.
  Elections (timeout, pre-vote, votes, win) are one step with every member that would vote. A higher term carried
  on a message (an AppendEntries reply or a RequestVote) is its own step (`TermProp`). So a message between lease
  nodes is never delivered after a link change, never duplicated, never reordered with others between the same
  pair. This is the main abstraction; see Limitations.
- **Repeated timeouts are collapsed.** A needed election takes the smallest term at which a quorum would vote; a
  pre-vote rejected for a stale term teaches the higher term (as etcd's PreVote does), so terms do not gate it.
- **Client and operator messages.** A client's request and an operator's reconfiguration request arrive in the step
  they are sent, if the link is up (lost otherwise; a client whose request survives nowhere sends it again, which
  abstracts its retry timer). A receiver's reply reaches its operator in the step it is sent, or is lost and resent.
  A grant reply to a running client arrives in the step it is sent; to a paused client it stays in flight until the
  client resumes. Writes, reads and their replies are explicit in-flight messages (they may be reordered and may
  arrive after a link goes down); storage holds its replies in an outbox that a crash empties.
- **Messages to a crashed process are lost**; a restarted process does not receive what was sent while it was down.
- **No clocks.** No protocol decision reads a clock: the grantor does not wait for expiry (the contract allows
  non-exclusive grants) and Raft's timers are abstracted by nondeterminism. A clock step (F3.2) is recorded as a
  `Fault` with its size and changes no state, so every clock value is equivalent to every other for this model;
  "between steps clocks advance by any number of ticks" is covered because nothing depends on the number. The
  mutants that need a clock (P32, P41, P44, P47, P50, P53, P59, P62) add one.
- **Storage** is one process with a durable ledger and value (contract v3).
- **Integers** are TLA+ integers; TLC's term bound keeps them small; `Overflow` never occurs and is not modelled.

## Interpretations of the inputs

Each of these is a place where the inputs left a choice. None changes an input.

1. *Decider per proposal* (above). Consequence: a configuration whose receiver restarts amnesic before deciding is
   never decided (see Findings, P63).
2. *Agreed records.* A grant's decider records `Agreed` for each agreement to an undecided entry of its own term when
   it receives it (counted toward the grant's epoch if eligible, else `[]`); agreements arriving after the decision
   are not recorded. A configuration's receiver records `Agreed` for each agreement handed to it while its request
   is pending, with `counted_toward` the epochs among e, e+1 in which it is eligible (an amnesic incarnation's is
   `[]`, the re-admission evidence). Every `Agreed` names the node's `Agree` in `causes` (matched by node,
   incarnation and proposal).
3. *Grant inputs.* `agreed` (every recorded `Agreed`, by ref), `members` and `config_epoch` (the decider's current
   configuration), `grantor_term` (the decider's term), `last_token` (the highest token in the decider's log before
   the entry: what it knew when it chose the token). No grant reads a clock, so `clock` and `last_grant_at` are
   never recorded. No extra input names are used (`--extra-inputs` is not needed).
4. *Which epoch a request would occupy* is the receiver's current epoch plus one when it records the request. A
   leader starts it only as that epoch; if the receiver learns that epoch committed to another request it refuses
   `superseded` (the operator may send it again). `invalid` then `busy` are decided when the request is recorded.
5. *C1.1 across configurations* is checked as (a) no two grants share a token, (b) a higher epoch carries a higher
   token, and (c) in every node's log, decided grants appear in increasing token order (a node agrees in log order
   and decided entries are never removed); the trace-level form of (c) is checked by decision replay, part 2.
   Two grants with one term must come from one node incarnation, and at most one leader holds a term at a time.
6. *C1.2 and C2.1, "the highest token storage has accepted"*, are read against the history of accepted writes, not
   only the current ledger, so a ledger that loses its value is caught.
7. *C1.4 and C3.4 premises* are read as the schedule format's Rule L3 extended: after the last fault step of the
   schedule has been taken; the globally committed configuration (the highest decided epoch in the run); an
   eligible majority of it (and, for C3.4(b), of the requested set) up and pairwise connected with the receiver or
   with storage and the requester; no reconfiguration request pending at an up node for C1.4.
8. *Where the last fault depends on the obligation.* In P10 and P12 the last fault (P10: none after the grant to
   c2 if c2 is never granted; P12: the resume) is triggered by the very grant C1.4 would owe, so if the grant never
   comes the last fault never happens and C1.4 owes nothing. The model reports such a run as
   `UNEXPLAINED end unreachable`, not `FAIL`.
9. *Spurious elections* (asynchrony) are allowed only before the last fault: after it, messages arrive within a
   bound and a node that hears a leader does not time out.
10. *Selectors.* `grantor`, `holder` and `non-member` are resolved when the trigger fires, from the most recent
    `Grant` and the highest decided commit in the run; every `non-grantor` (and `non-member`) choice is explored;
    several `non-grantor` occurrences in one step denote one node. A schedule that names `grantor`/`holder` before
    any `request` step is rejected.
11. *`quiescent`* holds when every step has been taken, no message is in flight to a running process, storage's
    outbox is empty, no running client is waiting for a grant and no request is pending at an up receiver.
12. *The schedule's `bound: {events: N}`* is not used; TLC's bounds below replace it, and are reported.
13. *Incarnations in records*: a lease node's `inc` counts its amnesic restarts; a client's or storage's counts its
    restarts (schema v5); `env` and operators are 0.
14. *Values*: storage's initial value `null` is `"null"` in the model and `null` in the trace.
15. *Clock steps* are compiled to ticks (`step × L`) and must be whole (the format's rule).
16. *Removed nodes* keep running and keep their state (failure model, Configuration locus); they stop campaigning
    once they know they are not members.

## Bounds, and what each schedule must reach

Every exhaustive run is bounded by:
- **MaxTerm**: the highest term reachable before the last fault: `1 + L + Spur0`, where L counts the schedule's
  leader-loss steps (each run of consecutive lease-node crashes once, each partition, cut or drop, and one for any
  reconfiguration). After the last fault the cap rises by one term per lease node, so that elections the faults
  force can still happen; a terminal state stuck at the cap is reported `UNEXPLAINED bound`, never `PASS` or `FAIL`.
- **Spur0 = 1**: one spurious election (a timeout while a leader is still reachable) before the last fault.
- The schedule itself: its steps, processes and requests (tokens and grants grow only with requests and terms).
No other constraint is applied; there is no depth bound. `RESULTS.md` lists, per schedule, what it must reach
(epochs, restarts, amnesic restarts, clock steps and their sizes in ticks, grants, the elections its faults force),
the bounds it ran at, the number of states explored, and what its witness trace actually reached. A schedule whose
witness reaches its end shows the bounded space contains a behaviour that does everything the schedule asks.

## Liveness (C1.4, C3.4), and the fairness it rests on

C1.4 and C3.4 are checked in **terminal form**. Every action of the model changes the state monotonically (terms,
logs, decided-configuration knowledge, the schedule position, consumed messages, histories); no action undoes
another. So the reachable state graph has no cycle, every behaviour ends in a terminal state where nothing is
enabled, and at a terminal state weak fairness of every action holds vacuously. Under weak fairness of every action,
"eventually P" then holds in every behaviour if and only if P holds in every reachable terminal state. The checked
specification is `SpecL == Init /\ [][Next \/ Idle]_vars` with `Idle` (stuttering) enabled exactly when no
obligation is unmet; TLC's deadlock check then finds exactly the terminal states that leave a C1.4 or C3.4
obligation unmet, and a one-state TLC run classifies which (`Stuck14`, `Stuck34`, `StuckBound`).

I validated the terminal form against TLC's temporal check of `C1_4` under explicit fairness (`LiveSpec`,
`live.cfg`) on small schedules: the two agree on P26 (unmutated: holds; P26 mutant: violated), H10 (holds),
P10 (holds) and the original P10 mutant (holds: see interpretation 8). The temporal check is ~1,000 times slower
here (`ENABLED` for ~80 fairness conditions), which is why it is not the default.

The fairness the terminal form amounts to is weak fairness of every action. Every action of the model is enabled by
the acting process's own state and by links that are up at that moment: an AppendEntries needs leader→follower up,
an election needs the candidate and its voters connected, a forward needs the link to the leader, a delivery needs
the message in flight to a running process. No action requires hearing from a peer across a link that is down, and
the actions whose enablement is "nothing was heard" (an election timeout when no leader is heard; CheckQuorum's
step-down when a majority is not heard) depend only on the acting node's own state. Spurious timeouts are not fair
and stop at the last fault. Liveness therefore rests on: weak fairness of every action (justified by "after the last
fault, a message between two connected processes is delivered within a bound", failure model v3) and the absence
of spurious elections after the last fault (the same clause: timers longer than the bound). No liveness result
rests on fairness across a down link.

## Mutations

`mutations/make.py` generates one copy of `Lease.tla` per pair with one deliberate break on the enforcing path of
the pair's clause, marked `\* mutation: P<n>` at the break and named in the module header; `mutations/MUTATIONS.md`
lists them. Mutants that need state the model does not keep add it as `aux` (clock offsets for the F3.2 pairs;
pending client operations for the C1.3 and C2.2 pairs that fabricate an outcome). For C3.5 the break makes a
decision consult an input it does not record (storage reading a link state or its own clock; a commit reading
incarnations it did not record), which both the model's `C3_5` rule and the steward's decision-replay check catch.

  winnable term (`Elect`).
- **P42, FAIL C3.4**: a pre-vote was refused when the voter's term exceeded the pre-candidate's term + 1, leaving
  no node able to elect after the leader that held the change restarted amnesic. In Raft's PreVote the rejection
  carries the higher term and the pre-candidate retries. Fix: terms do not gate the pre-vote.

forwarding, immediate client/operator messages, a VIEW without the last step's events, the terminal form of
liveness), or made spurious elections atomic; the P10 mutation was redesigned after both checkers showed the
original could not fail (interpretation 8). All of this is in the commit history.

## Findings

  n2 (incarnation 0); n2 restarts amnesic; the entry is then replicated and committed through n2#1, n3 and n4; its
  only decider no longer exists, the change stays undecided in every log, the leader cannot start r2, and r2
  (pending at n1, every premise of C3.4(b) holding) is never committed or refused. In the world I predicted
  (the entry committed before the receiver's amnesic restart, its decision possibly recorded and not yet heard of)
  I believe no protocol keeps both C3.1's single decision per epoch and C3.4: no live process can tell "decided
  and not yet announced" from "never decided", so deciding again risks a second decided record for epoch 1, taking
  epoch 1 for r2 risks two configurations for it, and waiting blocks r2. In the world TLC shows the entry was not
  yet committed when the receiver restarted, so a protocol that could abandon an appended joint entry would pass;
  Raft cannot. The verdict stays FAIL (unexplained until a judge discriminates); it is a property of the contract's
  single-decider rule under F3.3 at the decider as much as of this design.
- **P10 and P12: C1.4 is vacuous where the last fault waits on the grant** (interpretation 8); their mutants cannot
  fail C1.4 by design of the schedule. (The P10 mutation was moved to elections, which bite after the last fault.)

## Declared limitations

Shapes of schedule this model would fail or could not check, and why I left them:
- **Stale messages between lease nodes.** Because lease-to-lease messages are atomic, the model cannot show a
  failure that needs an AppendEntries, vote or acknowledgement sent before a link change and delivered after it, a
  duplicated one, or one reordered behind a later one. Raft is designed for those, and modelling them made the
  state space unmanageable (P1 alone exceeded 25 million states at depth 18).
- **Duplicated client, storage and operator messages** are not modelled (sets, not bags).
- **Bounded asynchrony.** One spurious election before the last fault, and MaxTerm as above. A failure needing two
  spurious elections, or more elections than the faults force plus one, is outside the space.
- **No clocks in the protocol.** A schedule whose failure depends on a decision reading a clock cannot fail here
  (none does in this design); conversely a clock-based lease protocol is not what is modelled.
- **Liveness under the terminal form** relies on the reachable graph being acyclic (argued above, validated on
  four small schedules with the temporal check, not proved). A livelock that keeps raising terms after the last
  fault is reported `UNEXPLAINED bound`, not `FAIL`.
- **C3.5 across runs** is checked over the traces the runner exports (one shortest witness or counterexample plus
  `MODEL_SIMS` random behaviours per schedule), not over every behaviour; within the model, every decision of every
  explored behaviour is checked against the rule of its recorded inputs (`C3_5`).
- **Large schedules take minutes**: P31 (5 nodes, two operators) ~9 million states, P52 (6 nodes) ~12 million;
  `run.sh --all` takes about an hour on 48 cores. A larger schedule (more lease nodes, more requests, more faults)
  may exceed `TLC_TIMEOUT` and is then reported `UNEXPLAINED bound (TLC time limit ...)`.
- **The inputs I could not use.** This checkout also contains `contract/v2.md`, `failure-model/v1.md` and `v2.md`,
  `tests/pairs-v1.md` to `v3.md`, `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` and `scripts/hooks/`, which the brief says are absent;
  I did not read them (I saw the first lines of `pyproject.toml` while checking the toolchain, and nothing else).

This directory is the model half of every pair in `tests/pairs-v4.md` (P1 to P33, P40 to P54, P58 to P63), written
from `contract/v3.md`, `failure-model/v3.md`, the schedule format (v2.2 to v5), the observability schema (v1 to v5)
and the steward's decision-replay check, and nothing else. Predictions were committed before any of it existed
(`PREDICTIONS.md`, commit `be79db9`). Results are in `RESULTS.md`; this file says what was built, how to run it, what
the model abstracts, how I read the inputs, the bounds and what they reach, and what I believe it cannot show.

## How to run

```
model-regen/run.sh P1                 # one schedule: prints PASS, FAIL <clause> or UNEXPLAINED <reason>
model-regen/run.sh --all              # every testbed/schedules/*.yaml (any name the format accepts)
model-regen/run.sh --mutations        # every pair's mutant on its pair's shared schedule
model-regen/run.sh P31 --spur 0 --max-term 3 --sims 4    # bounds and the number of random witness traces
```

Requirements: Java 21, `/opt/tlaplus/tla2tools.jar` (TLC 2.19), `uv` with `pyyaml==6.0.3` in its offline cache.
Environment: `TLC_HEAP` (default `10g`), `TLC_WORKERS` (48), `TLC_TIMEOUT` seconds per TLC run (5400),
`MODEL_SIMS` random witness traces per schedule (8). Generated TLC inputs go to `tmp/model-regen/<name>/` (never
committed); each run writes `observe/<run>.jsonl` (the counterexample if there is one, otherwise the shortest
behaviour that reaches the schedule's end) and `model-regen/results/schedules/<name>/` (verdict, TLC tails, traces,
the decision-replay report). `run.sh` resolves `testbed/schedules/<name>.yaml` and accepts any schedule in the format;
a schedule the format does not allow is reported `UNEXPLAINED rejected <reason>`.

One run of `run.sh <name>`:
1. `compile.py` turns the YAML into `MC.tla` (the schedule as TLA+ constants) and three TLC configurations.
2. TLC explores, breadth first and exhaustively within the bounds below, `SpecL` against every safety invariant
   and per-step property, and the liveness clauses in terminal form (see Liveness). A violation is `FAIL <clause>`
   with its counterexample exported; a terminal state with an unmet C1.4 or C3.4 obligation is `FAIL C1.4` or
   `FAIL C3.4`, or `UNEXPLAINED bound` if it sits at the term bound.
3. TLC finds the shortest behaviour that reaches the schedule's end (`NotEnded` as an invariant); none means
   `UNEXPLAINED end unreachable` (Rule E2: only when no violation was witnessed).
4. TLC samples `MODEL_SIMS` more behaviours to the end at random (simulation mode), for C3.5 across runs.
5. `observe/decision_replay.py` runs on every exported trace of the run; a report is `FAIL` with the clause it names
   (`C3.5` for equal inputs with unequal outcomes).

Files: `Lease.tla` (the model), `compile.py` (schedule compiler), `export.py` (TLC trace to `observe/<run>.jsonl`),

   schedule has been taken; the globally committed configuration (the highest decided epoch in the run); an
   eligible majority of it (and, for C3.4(b), of the requested set) up and pairwise connected with the receiver or
   with storage and the requester; no reconfiguration request pending at an up node for C1.4.
8. *Where the last fault depends on the obligation.* In P10 and P12 the last fault (P10: none after the grant to
   c2 if c2 is never granted; P12: the resume) is triggered by the very grant C1.4 would owe, so if the grant never
   comes the last fault never happens and C1.4 owes nothing. The model reports such a run as
   `UNEXPLAINED end unreachable`, not `FAIL`.
9. *Spurious elections* (asynchrony) are allowed only before the last fault: after it, messages arrive within a
   bound and a node that hears a leader does not time out.
10. *Selectors.* `grantor`, `holder` and `non-member` are resolved when the trigger fires, from the most recent
    `Grant` and the highest decided commit in the run; every `non-grantor` (and `non-member`) choice is explored;
    several `non-grantor` occurrences in one step denote one node. A schedule that names `grantor`/`holder` before
    any `request` step is rejected.
11. *`quiescent`* holds when every step has been taken, no message is in flight to a running process, storage's
    outbox is empty, no running client is waiting for a grant and no request is pending at an up receiver.
12. *The schedule's `bound: {events: N}`* is not used; TLC's bounds below replace it, and are reported.
13. *Incarnations in records*: a lease node's `inc` counts its amnesic restarts; a client's or storage's counts its
    restarts (schema v5); `env` and operators are 0.
14. *Values*: storage's initial value `null` is `"null"` in the model and `null` in the trace.
15. *Clock steps* are compiled to ticks (`step × L`) and must be whole (the format's rule).
16. *Removed nodes* keep running and keep their state (failure model, Configuration locus); they stop campaigning
    once they know they are not members.

## Bounds, and what each schedule must reach

Every exhaustive run is bounded by:
- **MaxTerm**: the highest term reachable before the last fault: `1 + L + Spur0`, where L counts the schedule's
  leader-loss steps (each run of consecutive lease-node crashes once, each partition, cut or drop, and one for any
  reconfiguration). After the last fault the cap rises by one term per lease node, so that elections the faults
  force can still happen; a terminal state stuck at the cap is reported `UNEXPLAINED bound`, never `PASS` or `FAIL`.
- **Spur0 = 1**: one spurious election (a timeout while a leader is still reachable) before the last fault.
- The schedule itself: its steps, processes and requests (tokens and grants grow only with requests and terms).
No other constraint is applied; there is no depth bound. `RESULTS.md` lists, per schedule, what it must reach
(epochs, restarts, amnesic restarts, clock steps and their sizes in ticks, grants, the elections its faults force),
the bounds it ran at, the number of states explored, and what its witness trace actually reached. A schedule whose
witness reaches its end shows the bounded space contains a behaviour that does everything the schedule asks.

## Liveness (C1.4, C3.4), and the fairness it rests on

C1.4 and C3.4 are checked in **terminal form**. Every action of the model changes the state monotonically (terms,
logs, decided-configuration knowledge, the schedule position, consumed messages, histories); no action undoes
another. So the reachable state graph has no cycle, every behaviour ends in a terminal state where nothing is
enabled, and at a terminal state weak fairness of every action holds vacuously. Under weak fairness of every action,
"eventually P" then holds in every behaviour if and only if P holds in every reachable terminal state. The checked
specification is `SpecL == Init /\ [][Next \/ Idle]_vars` with `Idle` (stuttering) enabled exactly when no
obligation is unmet; TLC's deadlock check then finds exactly the terminal states that leave a C1.4 or C3.4
obligation unmet, and a one-state TLC run classifies which (`Stuck14`, `Stuck34`, `StuckBound`).

I validated the terminal form against TLC's temporal check of `C1_4` under explicit fairness (`LiveSpec`,
`live.cfg`) on small schedules: the two agree on P26 (unmutated: holds; P26 mutant: violated), H10 (holds),
P10 (holds) and the original P10 mutant (holds: see interpretation 8). The temporal check is ~1,000 times slower
here (`ENABLED` for ~80 fairness conditions), which is why it is not the default.

The fairness the terminal form amounts to is weak fairness of every action. Every action of the model is enabled by
the acting process's own state and by links that are up at that moment: an AppendEntries needs leader→follower up,
an election needs the candidate and its voters connected, a forward needs the link to the leader, a delivery needs
the message in flight to a running process. No action requires hearing from a peer across a link that is down, and
the actions whose enablement is "nothing was heard" (an election timeout when no leader is heard; CheckQuorum's
step-down when a majority is not heard) depend only on the acting node's own state. Spurious timeouts are not fair
and stop at the last fault. Liveness therefore rests on: weak fairness of every action (justified by "after the last
fault, a message between two connected processes is delivered within a bound", failure model v3) and the absence
of spurious elections after the last fault (the same clause: timers longer than the bound). No liveness result
rests on fairness across a down link.

## Mutations

`mutations/make.py` generates one copy of `Lease.tla` per pair with one deliberate break on the enforcing path of
the pair's clause, marked `\* mutation: P<n>` at the break and named in the module header; `mutations/MUTATIONS.md`
lists them. Mutants that need state the model does not keep add it as `aux` (clock offsets for the F3.2 pairs;
pending client operations for the C1.3 and C2.2 pairs that fabricate an outcome). For C3.5 the break makes a
decision consult an input it does not record (storage reading a link state or its own clock; a commit reading
incarnations it did not record), which both the model's `C3_5` rule and the steward's decision-replay check catch.
Results are in `RESULTS.md`.

## Development history before the first version (recorded, not hidden)

The model failed shared schedules twice while it was being built; both times the old behaviour misread the
published protocol (and so C1.4/C3.4), and the counterexamples are kept under `results/dev-history/`:
- **P10, FAIL C1.4**: a node left with a vote for itself in term 2 by a spurious timeout could not vote for anyone in
  term 2, and my atomic election only tried term+1. Raft times out again. Fix: an election takes the smallest
  winnable term (`Elect`).
- **P42, FAIL C3.4**: a pre-vote was refused when the voter's term exceeded the pre-candidate's term + 1, leaving
  no node able to elect after the leader that held the change restarted amnesic. In Raft's PreVote the rejection
  carries the higher term and the pre-candidate retries. Fix: terms do not gate the pre-vote.
Other changes while building reduced state space without changing behaviours the clauses distinguish (atomic
forwarding, immediate client/operator messages, a VIEW without the last step's events, the terminal form of
liveness), or made spurious elections atomic; the P10 mutation was redesigned after both checkers showed the
original could not fail (interpretation 8). All of this is in the commit history.

## Findings

- **P63: FAIL C3.4, predicted.** In the counterexample n1 (leader) appends r1's joint entry, whose receiver is
  n2 (incarnation 0); n2 restarts amnesic; the entry is then replicated and committed through n2#1, n3 and n4; its
  only decider no longer exists, the change stays undecided in every log, the leader cannot start r2, and r2
  (pending at n1, every premise of C3.4(b) holding) is never committed or refused. In the world I predicted
  (the entry committed before the receiver's amnesic restart, its decision possibly recorded and not yet heard of)
  I believe no protocol keeps both C3.1's single decision per epoch and C3.4: no live process can tell "decided
  and not yet announced" from "never decided", so deciding again risks a second decided record for epoch 1, taking
  epoch 1 for r2 risks two configurations for it, and waiting blocks r2. In the world TLC shows the entry was not
  yet committed when the receiver restarted, so a protocol that could abandon an appended joint entry would pass;
  Raft cannot. The verdict stays FAIL (unexplained until a judge discriminates); it is a property of the contract's
  single-decider rule under F3.3 at the decider as much as of this design.
- **P10 and P12: C1.4 is vacuous where the last fault waits on the grant** (interpretation 8); their mutants cannot
  fail C1.4 by design of the schedule. (The P10 mutation was moved to elections, which bite after the last fault.)

## Declared limitations

Shapes of schedule this model would fail or could not check, and why I left them:
- **Stale messages between lease nodes.** Because lease-to-lease messages are atomic, the model cannot show a
  failure that needs an AppendEntries, vote or acknowledgement sent before a link change and delivered after it, a
  duplicated one, or one reordered behind a later one. Raft is designed for those, and modelling them made the
  state space unmanageable (P1 alone exceeded 25 million states at depth 18).
- **Duplicated client, storage and operator messages** are not modelled (sets, not bags).
- **Bounded asynchrony.** One spurious election before the last fault, and MaxTerm as above. A failure needing two
  spurious elections, or more elections than the faults force plus one, is outside the space.
- **No clocks in the protocol.** A schedule whose failure depends on a decision reading a clock cannot fail here
  (none does in this design); conversely a clock-based lease protocol is not what is modelled.
- **Liveness under the terminal form** relies on the reachable graph being acyclic (argued above, validated on
  four small schedules with the temporal check, not proved). A livelock that keeps raising terms after the last
  fault is reported `UNEXPLAINED bound`, not `FAIL`.
- **C3.5 across runs** is checked over the traces the runner exports (one shortest witness or counterexample plus
  `MODEL_SIMS` random behaviours per schedule), not over every behaviour; within the model, every decision of every
  explored behaviour is checked against the rule of its recorded inputs (`C3_5`).
- **Large schedules take minutes**: P31 (5 nodes, two operators) ~9 million states, P52 (6 nodes) ~12 million;
  `run.sh --all` takes about an hour on 48 cores. A larger schedule (more lease nodes, more requests, more faults)
  may exceed `TLC_TIMEOUT` and is then reported `UNEXPLAINED bound (TLC time limit ...)`.
- **The inputs I could not use.** This checkout also contains `contract/v2.md`, `failure-model/v1.md` and `v2.md`,
  `tests/pairs-v1.md` to `v3.md`, `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` and `scripts/hooks/`, which the brief says are absent;
  I did not read them (I saw the first lines of `pyproject.toml` while checking the toolchain, and nothing else).

derives: C1.1, C1.2, C1.3, C1.4, C2.1, C2.2, C3.1, C3.4, C3.5, C3.7, C3.8, F1.1, F1.2, F1.3, F2.1, F2.2, F3.1, F3.2,

import json
import os
import re
import subprocess
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, HERE)

for ps, c in [('1 2 3 19 20 46 47 48', 'C1.1'), ('4 5 6 21 22 49 50 51', 'C1.2'), ('7 8 9 23 24', 'C1.3'),

    for p in ps.split():
        PAIR_CLAUSE['P' + p] = c


def predicted(name):
    """derives: C3.4 -- the unmutated prediction"""
    return 'FAIL C3.4' if name == 'P63' else 'PASS'


def key(n):
    m = re.match(r'P(\d+)$', n)
    return (0, int(m.group(1))) if m else (1, n)


def main():
    base = os.path.join(HERE, 'results')
    rows, mrows = [], []
    for d in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(base, 'schedules', '*')), key=lambda p: key(os.path.basename(p))):
        f = os.path.join(d, 'result.json')
        if not os.path.exists(f):

    out = ['# Results (model side)', '',

           '## Shared schedules, unmutated model', '',
           '| Schedule | Verdict | Predicted | Match | Distinct states | Depth | Seconds | MaxTerm / spurious | '
           'Witness length | Random traces | Decision replay |',
           '|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|']
    for n, v, p, st, w, sims, rep, mt, sp in rows:
        out.append(f"| {n} | {v} | {p} | {'yes' if v == p else '**no**'} | {st.get('distinct', '-')} | "
                   f"{st.get('depth', '-')} | {st.get('seconds', '-')} | {mt} / {sp} | {w.get('length', '-')} | "
                   f"{sims if sims is not None else '-'} | {rep} |")
    out += ['', '## Mutations (each on its pair\'s shared schedule)', '',
            '| Pair | Mutant verdict | Predicted | Match | Distinct states | Seconds |', '|---|---|---|---|---|---|']
    for n, v, p, st in mrows:
        out.append(f"| {n} | {v} | {p} | {'yes' if v == p else '**no**'} | {st.get('distinct', '-')} | "

    out += ['', '## Reach: what each schedule needs, the bounds it ran at, what its witness reached', '']
    r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, os.path.join(HERE, 'reach.py')], capture_output=True, text=True)
    out.append(r.stdout)
    print('\n'.join(out))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

1	# model-regen: the TLA+ model side of tupay, built fresh from contract v3 and failure model v3
2	
3	derives: C1.1, C1.2, C1.3, C1.4, C2.1, C2.2, C3.1, C3.4, C3.5, C3.7, C3.8, F1.1, F1.2, F1.3, F2.1, F2.2, F3.1, F3.2, F3.3
4	
5	This directory is the model half of every pair in `tests/pairs-v4.md` (P1 to P33, P40 to P54, P58 to P63), written
6	from `contract/v3.md`, `failure-model/v3.md`, the schedule format (v2.2 to v5), the observability schema (v1 to v5)
7	and the steward's decision-replay check, and nothing else. Predictions were committed before any of it existed
8	(`PREDICTIONS.md`, commit `be79db9`). Results are in `RESULTS.md`; this file says what was built, how to run it, what
9	the model abstracts, how I read the inputs, the bounds and what they reach, and what I believe it cannot show.
10	
11	## How to run
12	
13	```
14	model-regen/run.sh P1                 # one schedule: prints PASS, FAIL <clause> or UNEXPLAINED <reason>
15	model-regen/run.sh --all              # every testbed/schedules/*.yaml (any name the format accepts)
16	model-regen/run.sh --mutations        # every pair's mutant on its pair's shared schedule
17	model-regen/run.sh P31 --spur 0 --max-term 3 --sims 4    # bounds and the number of random witness traces
18	```
19	
20	Requirements: Java 21, `/opt/tlaplus/tla2tools.jar` (TLC 2.19), `uv` with `pyyaml==6.0.3` in its offline cache.
21	Environment: `TLC_HEAP` (default `10g`), `TLC_WORKERS` (48), `TLC_TIMEOUT` seconds per TLC run (5400),
22	`MODEL_SIMS` random witness traces per schedule (8). Generated TLC inputs go to `tmp/model-regen/<name>/` (never
23	committed); each run writes `observe/<run>.jsonl` (the counterexample if there is one, otherwise the shortest
24	behaviour that reaches the schedule's end) and `model-regen/results/schedules/<name>/` (verdict, TLC tails, traces,
25	the decision-replay report). `run.sh` resolves `testbed/schedules/<name>.yaml` and accepts any schedule in the format;
26	a schedule the format does not allow is reported `UNEXPLAINED rejected <reason>`.
27	
28	One run of `run.sh <name>`:
29	1. `compile.py` turns the YAML into `MC.tla` (the schedule as TLA+ constants) and three TLC configurations.
30	2. TLC explores, breadth first and exhaustively within the bounds below, `SpecL` against every safety invariant
31	   and per-step property, and the liveness clauses in terminal form (see Liveness). A violation is `FAIL <clause>`
32	   with its counterexample exported; a terminal state with an unmet C1.4 or C3.4 obligation is `FAIL C1.4` or
33	   `FAIL C3.4`, or `UNEXPLAINED bound` if it sits at the term bound.
34	3. TLC finds the shortest behaviour that reaches the schedule's end (`NotEnded` as an invariant); none means
35	   `UNEXPLAINED end unreachable` (Rule E2: only when no violation was witnessed).
36	4. TLC samples `MODEL_SIMS` more behaviours to the end at random (simulation mode), for C3.5 across runs.
37	5. `observe/decision_replay.py` runs on every exported trace of the run; a report is `FAIL` with the clause it names
38	   (`C3.5` for equal inputs with unequal outcomes).
39	
40	Files: `Lease.tla` (the model), `compile.py` (schedule compiler), `export.py` (TLC trace to `observe/<run>.jsonl`),
41	`run.py`/`run.sh` (runner; `run.sh --reach` runs the reach probes), `reach.py` and `report.py` (the reach table and
42	`RESULTS.md`), `mutations/make.py` (generates `mutations/Lease_P<n>.tla`,
43	one deliberate break per pair, listed in `mutations/MUTATIONS.md`), `tlc.sh` (a bare TLC launcher used while
44	building), `PREDICTIONS.md`, `RESULTS.md`, `results/`.
45	
46	## The protocol followed
47	
48	**Raft with joint consensus**: D. Ongaro and J. Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm",
49	USENIX ATC 2014, sections 5 (leader election, log replication, safety) and 6 (cluster membership changes by joint
50	consensus); with **PreVote** and **CheckQuorum** from D. Ongaro, *Consensus: Bridging Theory and Practice*, PhD
51	thesis, Stanford University, 2014, sections 9.6 and 6.2. The model is a Raft abstraction in the style of published
52	atomic-quorum specifications: an election is one step, an AppendEntries and its acknowledgement are one step
53	(see Abstractions).
54	
55	A grant is a Raft log entry `(client, token, lifetime, config_epoch, term)`; a membership change from epoch e to
56	e+1 is a joint entry (C_old,new) carrying the new members and the request; leaders also append Raft's no-op on
57	election when they inherit an undecided change (paper, section 8).
58	
59	**Amnesic restart (F3.3).** The thesis (section 3.8) says a server that loses its persistent state cannot safely
60	rejoin under its old identity and can be added back as a new server through a membership change; until then it
61	behaves as a non-voting member (section 4.2.1). That is what the model does: an amnesic restart starts incarnation
62	i+1 with an empty log, term 0, no vote, and only the deployment's knowledge (its name, the lease nodes, the initial
63	configuration). Its acknowledgements are recorded but count toward no majority, its votes and pre-votes count for
64	nothing, and it may not start an election, until a commit that lists it and whose decider recorded this
65	incarnation's agreement re-admits it (contract v3, "Re-admission"). It stays in every denominator.
66	
67	**Where the protocol is adapted to the contract** (each is a reading of the contract, listed again under
68	Interpretations):
69	- *Who decides.* Contract v3 makes a commit a decision recorded once, by one node (`decided: true` exactly once per
70	  epoch). In Raft every leader that advances its commit index "learns" commitment, so two leaders can each believe
71	  they decided the same entry. The model therefore names one decider per proposal:
72	  - a **grant** is decided only by the leader that created its entry, from acknowledgements in its own term (Raft's
73	    direct commitment rule); an entry of an earlier term that a later leader commits indirectly is never decided
74	    and its token is dead (the client asks again);
75	  - a **configuration** is decided by the request's **receiver**, acting as a distinguished learner (L. Lamport,
76	    "Paxos Made Simple", SIGACT News 2001, section 2.3): a leader that knows the joint entry is committed (it
77	    counted joint majorities over an entry of its own term at or after it) hands the receiver the agreements it
78	    counted, possibly relayed by one node; the receiver records them as `Agreed` and decides when they form
79	    eligible majorities of the old and the new membership (C3.8).
80	- *C_new is implied.* Raft appends C_new after C_old,new commits; here a node uses the new membership alone once it
81	  knows epoch e+1 decided, and the joint one while the entry is in its log undecided. A leader not in the new
82	  membership steps down when it learns the decision.
83	- *Grants pause during a change.* A leader proposes no grant while a configuration entry in its log is undecided,
84	  and a grant is decided only under the decider's current configuration (C3.7).
85	- *A grant proposal carries its Raft entry term* (the contract's proposal fields plus `term`), so two entries with
86	  one token from different leaders are different proposals.
87	- *Requests reach a leader through a member.* A non-leader that receives a client's request or an operator's
88	  request passes it to a leader it reaches (directly, or through one member that reaches one), as Raft followers
89	  redirect; the receiver stays the node that records the outcome and answers the operator. A grant reply goes
90	  straight to the client, or back through the node that forwarded the request if the decider cannot reach the
91	  client (H9).
92	
93	## Abstractions (what the model does not represent, and why)
94	
95	- **Messages between lease nodes are atomic.** An AppendEntries and the follower's acknowledgement are one step,
96	  taken only while leader→follower is up; the acknowledgement is lost if follower→leader is down at that moment.
97	  Elections (timeout, pre-vote, votes, win) are one step with every member that would vote. A higher term carried
98	  on a message (an AppendEntries reply or a RequestVote) is its own step (`TermProp`). So a message between lease
99	  nodes is never delivered after a link change, never duplicated, never reordered with others between the same
100	  pair. This is the main abstraction; see Limitations.
101	- **Repeated timeouts are collapsed.** A needed election takes the smallest term at which a quorum would vote; a
102	  pre-vote rejected for a stale term teaches the higher term (as etcd's PreVote does), so terms do not gate it.
103	- **Client and operator messages.** A client's request and an operator's reconfiguration request arrive in the step
104	  they are sent, if the link is up (lost otherwise; a client whose request survives nowhere sends it again, which
105	  abstracts its retry timer). A receiver's reply reaches its operator in the step it is sent, or is lost and resent.
106	  A grant reply to a running client arrives in the step it is sent; to a paused client it stays in flight until the
107	  client resumes. Writes, reads and their replies are explicit in-flight messages (they may be reordered and may
108	  arrive after a link goes down); storage holds its replies in an outbox that a crash empties.
109	- **Messages to a crashed process are lost**; a restarted process does not receive what was sent while it was down.
110	- **No clocks.** No protocol decision reads a clock: the grantor does not wait for expiry (the contract allows
111	  non-exclusive grants) and Raft's timers are abstracted by nondeterminism. A clock step (F3.2) is recorded as a
112	  `Fault` with its size and changes no state, so every clock value is equivalent to every other for this model;
113	  "between steps clocks advance by any number of ticks" is covered because nothing depends on the number. The
114	  mutants that need a clock (P32, P41, P44, P47, P50, P53, P59, P62) add one.
115	- **Storage** is one process with a durable ledger and value (contract v3).
116	- **Integers** are TLA+ integers; TLC's term bound keeps them small; `Overflow` never occurs and is not modelled.
117	
118	## Interpretations of the inputs
119	
120	Each of these is a place where the inputs left a choice. None changes an input.
121	
122	1. *Decider per proposal* (above). Consequence: a configuration whose receiver restarts amnesic before deciding is
123	   never decided (see Findings, P63).
124	2. *Agreed records.* A grant's decider records `Agreed` for each agreement to an undecided entry of its own term when
125	   it receives it (counted toward the grant's epoch if eligible, else `[]`); agreements arriving after the decision
126	   are not recorded. A configuration's receiver records `Agreed` for each agreement handed to it while its request
127	   is pending, with `counted_toward` the epochs among e, e+1 in which it is eligible (an amnesic incarnation's is
128	   `[]`, the re-admission evidence). Every `Agreed` names the node's `Agree` in `causes` (matched by node,
129	   incarnation and proposal).
130	3. *Grant inputs.* `agreed` (every recorded `Agreed`, by ref), `members` and `config_epoch` (the decider's current
131	   configuration), `grantor_term` (the decider's term), `last_token` (the highest token in the decider's log before
132	   the entry: what it knew when it chose the token). No grant reads a clock, so `clock` and `last_grant_at` are
133	   never recorded. No extra input names are used (`--extra-inputs` is not needed).
134	4. *Which epoch a request would occupy* is the receiver's current epoch plus one when it records the request. A
135	   leader starts it only as that epoch; if the receiver learns that epoch committed to another request it refuses
136	   `superseded` (the operator may send it again). `invalid` then `busy` are decided when the request is recorded.
137	5. *C1.1 across configurations* is checked as (a) no two grants share a token, (b) a higher epoch carries a higher
138	   token, and (c) in every node's log, decided grants appear in increasing token order (a node agrees in log order
139	   and decided entries are never removed); the trace-level form of (c) is checked by decision replay, part 2.
140	   Two grants with one term must come from one node incarnation, and at most one leader holds a term at a time.
141	6. *C1.2 and C2.1, "the highest token storage has accepted"*, are read against the history of accepted writes, not
142	   only the current ledger, so a ledger that loses its value is caught. They are "only if" clauses: storage's
143	   rejecting *only* below the ledger is v3's fixed rule, which the contract says C1.2 and C2.1 permit and C3.5 needs,
144	   so that half is checked under C3.5 (`C3_5`), not under C1.2/C2.1. (My first invariants checked it under C1.2 and
145	   C2.1; the P43 and P44 mutants, which make storage reject on an unrecorded input, showed the misattribution.)
146	7. *C1.4 and C3.4 premises* are read as the schedule format's Rule L3 extended: after the last fault step of the
147	   schedule has been taken; the globally committed configuration (the highest decided epoch in the run); an
148	   eligible majority of it (and, for C3.4(b), of the requested set) up and pairwise connected with the receiver or
149	   with storage and the requester; no reconfiguration request pending at an up node for C1.4.
150	8. *Where the last fault depends on the obligation.* In P10 and P12 the last fault (P10: none after the grant to
151	   c2 if c2 is never granted; P12: the resume) is triggered by the very grant C1.4 would owe, so if the grant never
152	   comes the last fault never happens and C1.4 owes nothing. The model reports such a run as
153	   `UNEXPLAINED end unreachable`, not `FAIL`.
154	9. *Spurious elections* (asynchrony) are allowed only before the last fault: after it, messages arrive within a
155	   bound and a node that hears a leader does not time out.
156	10. *Selectors.* `grantor`, `holder` and `non-member` are resolved when the trigger fires, from the most recent
157	    `Grant` and the highest decided commit in the run; every `non-grantor` (and `non-member`) choice is explored;
158	    several `non-grantor` occurrences in one step denote one node. A schedule that names `grantor`/`holder` before
159	    any `request` step is rejected.
160	11. *`quiescent`* holds when every step has been taken, no message is in flight to a running process, storage's
161	    outbox is empty, no running client is waiting for a grant and no request is pending at an up receiver.
162	12. *The schedule's `bound: {events: N}`* is not used; TLC's bounds below replace it, and are reported.
163	13. *Incarnations in records*: a lease node's `inc` counts its amnesic restarts; a client's or storage's counts its
164	    restarts (schema v5); `env` and operators are 0.
165	14. *Values*: storage's initial value `null` is `"null"` in the model and `null` in the trace.
166	15. *Clock steps* are compiled to ticks (`step × L`) and must be whole (the format's rule).
167	16. *Removed nodes* keep running and keep their state (failure model, Configuration locus); they stop campaigning
168	    once they know they are not members.
169	
170	## Bounds, and what each schedule must reach
171	
172	Every exhaustive run is bounded by:
173	- **MaxTerm**: the highest term reachable before the last fault: `1 + L + Spur0`, where L counts the schedule's
174	  leader-loss steps (each run of consecutive lease-node crashes once, each partition, cut or drop, and one for any
175	  reconfiguration). After the last fault the cap rises by one term per lease node, so that elections the faults
176	  force can still happen; a terminal state stuck at the cap is reported `UNEXPLAINED bound`, never `PASS` or `FAIL`.
177	- **Spur0 = 1**: one spurious election (a timeout while a leader is still reachable) before the last fault.
178	- The schedule itself: its steps, processes and requests (tokens and grants grow only with requests and terms).
179	No other constraint is applied; there is no depth bound. `RESULTS.md` lists, per schedule, what it must reach
180	(epochs, restarts, amnesic restarts, clock steps and their sizes in ticks, grants, the elections its faults force),
181	the bounds it ran at, the number of states explored, what its shortest witness reached, and **reach probes**: TLC
182	reachability checks, at the same bounds, of every epoch the schedule's valid requests allow (`ProbeEpoch(k)`), of one
183	grant per request (`ProbeGrants`), and of a re-admitting commit where an amnesic restart is followed by a request
184	(`ProbeReadmit`). Every probe that the schedule allows is reachable; the three "re-admission: unreachable" (P33, P42,
185	P60) are schedules whose later request omits the amnesic node, so re-admission is impossible there, as it should be.
186	A schedule whose witness reaches its end, and whose probes are reachable, shows that the bounded space contains the
187	behaviours the schedule asks for.
188	
189	## Liveness (C1.4, C3.4), and the fairness it rests on
190	
191	C1.4 and C3.4 are checked in **terminal form**. Every action of the model changes the state monotonically (terms,
192	logs, decided-configuration knowledge, the schedule position, consumed messages, histories); no action undoes
193	another. So the reachable state graph has no cycle, every behaviour ends in a terminal state where nothing is
194	enabled, and at a terminal state weak fairness of every action holds vacuously. Under weak fairness of every action,
195	"eventually P" then holds in every behaviour if and only if P holds in every reachable terminal state. The checked
196	specification is `SpecL == Init /\ [][Next \/ Idle]_vars` with `Idle` (stuttering) enabled exactly when no
197	obligation is unmet; TLC's deadlock check then finds exactly the terminal states that leave a C1.4 or C3.4
198	obligation unmet, and a one-state TLC run classifies which (`Stuck14`, `Stuck34`, `StuckBound`).
199	
200	I validated the terminal form against TLC's temporal check of `C1_4` under explicit fairness (`LiveSpec`,
201	`live.cfg`, `-lncheck final`) on small schedules (`results/liveness-crosscheck.txt`). The two agree on every case
202	tried: unmutated P10, P11, P25, P26, P54, H9 and H10 hold; the P11, P25, P26 and P54 mutants and the redesigned P10
203	mutant are violated; the original P10 mutant holds under both (interpretation 8). The temporal check is ~1,000 times slower
204	here (`ENABLED` for ~80 fairness conditions), which is why it is not the default.
205	
206	The fairness the terminal form amounts to is weak fairness of every action. Every action of the model is enabled by
207	the acting process's own state and by links that are up at that moment: an AppendEntries needs leader→follower up,
208	an election needs the candidate and its voters connected, a forward needs the link to the leader, a delivery needs
209	the message in flight to a running process. No action requires hearing from a peer across a link that is down, and
210	the actions whose enablement is "nothing was heard" (an election timeout when no leader is heard; CheckQuorum's
211	step-down when a majority is not heard) depend only on the acting node's own state. Spurious timeouts are not fair
212	and stop at the last fault. Liveness therefore rests on: weak fairness of every action (justified by "after the last
213	fault, a message between two connected processes is delivered within a bound", failure model v3) and the absence
214	of spurious elections after the last fault (the same clause: timers longer than the bound). No liveness result
215	rests on fairness across a down link.
216	
217	## Mutations
218	
219	`mutations/make.py` generates one copy of `Lease.tla` per pair with one deliberate break on the enforcing path of
220	the pair's clause, marked `\* mutation: P<n>` at the break and named in the module header; `mutations/MUTATIONS.md`
221	lists them. Mutants that need state the model does not keep add it as `aux` (clock offsets for the F3.2 pairs;
222	pending client operations for the C1.3 and C2.2 pairs that fabricate an outcome). For C3.5 the break makes a
223	decision consult an input it does not record (storage reading a link state or its own clock; a commit reading
224	incarnations it did not record), which both the model's `C3_5` rule and the steward's decision-replay check catch.
225	A mutant may break more than its pair's clause, and TLC stops at the first violation it meets; in mutation mode the
226	runner then checks the pair's own clause alone as well and reports both (`FAIL C1.1; FAIL C3.7 (pair clause,
227	checked alone)`). Mutants redesigned after a run are recorded in `mutations/MUTATIONS.md` and below. Results are in
228	`RESULTS.md`.
229	
230	## Development history before the first version (recorded, not hidden)
231	
232	The model failed shared schedules twice while it was being built; both times the old behaviour misread the
233	published protocol (and so C1.4/C3.4), and the counterexamples are kept under `results/dev-history/`:
234	- **P10, FAIL C1.4**: a node left with a vote for itself in term 2 by a spurious timeout could not vote for anyone in
235	  term 2, and my atomic election only tried term+1. Raft times out again. Fix: an election takes the smallest
236	  winnable term (`Elect`).
237	- **P42, FAIL C3.4**: a pre-vote was refused when the voter's term exceeded the pre-candidate's term + 1, leaving
238	  no node able to elect after the leader that held the change restarted amnesic. In Raft's PreVote the rejection
239	  carries the higher term and the pre-candidate retries. Fix: terms do not gate the pre-vote.
240	Other changes while building reduced state space without changing behaviours the clauses distinguish (atomic
241	forwarding, immediate client/operator messages, a VIEW without the last step's events, the terminal form of
242	liveness), or made spurious elections atomic. Mutations redesigned after a run: P10 (the first design, unanimous
243	grants, could not fail: interpretation 8; moved to unanimous elections); P63 (first "the old majority is not
244	required": ineffective on P63, where every majority of the new set contains one of the old; then "the receiver
245	counts an amnesic agreement": ineffective, because the leader hands over agreements only after counting eligible
246	majorities itself; finally both the leader's commit count and the receiver's decision judge eligibility by node).
247	All of this is in the commit history.
248	
249	## Findings
250	
251	- **P63: FAIL C3.4, predicted.** In the counterexample n1 (leader) appends r1's joint entry, whose receiver is
252	  n2 (incarnation 0); n2 restarts amnesic; the entry is then replicated and committed through n2#1, n3 and n4; its
253	  only decider no longer exists, the change stays undecided in every log, the leader cannot start r2, and r2
254	  (pending at n1, every premise of C3.4(b) holding) is never committed or refused. In the world I predicted
255	  (the entry committed before the receiver's amnesic restart, its decision possibly recorded and not yet heard of)
256	  I believe no protocol keeps both C3.1's single decision per epoch and C3.4: no live process can tell "decided
257	  and not yet announced" from "never decided", so deciding again risks a second decided record for epoch 1, taking
258	  epoch 1 for r2 risks two configurations for it, and waiting blocks r2. In the world TLC shows the entry was not
259	  yet committed when the receiver restarted, so a protocol that could abandon an appended joint entry would pass;
260	  Raft cannot. The verdict stays FAIL (unexplained until a judge discriminates); it is a property of the contract's
261	  single-decider rule under F3.3 at the decider as much as of this design.
262	- **P10 and P12: C1.4 is vacuous where the last fault waits on the grant** (interpretation 8); their mutants cannot
263	  fail C1.4 by design of the schedule. (The P10 mutation was moved to elections, which bite after the last fault.)
264	
265	## Declared limitations
266	
267	Shapes of schedule this model would fail or could not check, and why I left them:
268	- **Stale messages between lease nodes.** Because lease-to-lease messages are atomic, the model cannot show a
269	  failure that needs an AppendEntries, vote or acknowledgement sent before a link change and delivered after it, a
270	  duplicated one, or one reordered behind a later one. Raft is designed for those, and modelling them made the
271	  state space unmanageable (P1 alone exceeded 25 million states at depth 18).
272	- **Duplicated client, storage and operator messages** are not modelled (sets, not bags).
273	- **Bounded asynchrony.** One spurious election before the last fault, and MaxTerm as above. A failure needing two
274	  spurious elections, or more elections than the faults force plus one, is outside the space.
275	- **No clocks in the protocol.** A schedule whose failure depends on a decision reading a clock cannot fail here
276	  (none does in this design); conversely a clock-based lease protocol is not what is modelled.
277	- **Liveness under the terminal form** relies on the reachable graph being acyclic (argued above, validated on
278	  four small schedules with the temporal check, not proved). A livelock that keeps raising terms after the last
279	  fault is reported `UNEXPLAINED bound`, not `FAIL`.
280	- **C3.5 across runs** is checked over the traces the runner exports (one shortest witness or counterexample plus
281	  `MODEL_SIMS` random behaviours per schedule), not over every behaviour; within the model, every decision of every
282	  explored behaviour is checked against the rule of its recorded inputs (`C3_5`).
283	- **Large schedules take minutes**: P31 (5 nodes, two operators) ~9 million states, P52 (6 nodes) ~12 million;
284	  `run.sh --all` takes about an hour on 48 cores. A larger schedule (more lease nodes, more requests, more faults)
285	  may exceed `TLC_TIMEOUT` and is then reported `UNEXPLAINED bound (TLC time limit ...)`.
286	- **The inputs I could not use.** This checkout also contains `contract/v2.md`, `failure-model/v1.md` and `v2.md`,
287	  `tests/pairs-v1.md` to `v3.md`, `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` and `scripts/hooks/`, which the brief says are absent;
288	  I did not read them (I saw the first lines of `pyproject.toml` while checking the toolchain, and nothing else).
289

# model-regen: the TLA+ model side of tupay, built fresh from contract v3 and failure model v3

derives: C1.1, C1.2, C1.3, C1.4, C2.1, C2.2, C3.1, C3.4, C3.5, C3.7, C3.8, F1.1, F1.2, F1.3, F2.1, F2.2, F3.1, F3.2, F3.3

This directory is the model half of every pair in `tests/pairs-v4.md` (P1 to P33, P40 to P54, P58 to P63), written
from `contract/v3.md`, `failure-model/v3.md`, the schedule format (v2.2 to v5), the observability schema (v1 to v5)
and the steward's decision-replay check, and nothing else. Predictions were committed before any of it existed
(`PREDICTIONS.md`, commit `be79db9`). Results are in `RESULTS.md`; this file says what was built, how to run it, what
the model abstracts, how I read the inputs, the bounds and what they reach, and what I believe it cannot show.

## How to run

```
model-regen/run.sh P1                 # one schedule: prints PASS, FAIL <clause> or UNEXPLAINED <reason>
model-regen/run.sh --all              # every testbed/schedules/*.yaml (any name the format accepts)
model-regen/run.sh --mutations        # every pair's mutant on its pair's shared schedule
model-regen/run.sh P31 --spur 0 --max-term 3 --sims 4    # bounds and the number of random witness traces
```

Requirements: Java 21, `/opt/tlaplus/tla2tools.jar` (TLC 2.19), `uv` with `pyyaml==6.0.3` in its offline cache.
Environment: `TLC_HEAP` (default `10g`), `TLC_WORKERS` (48), `TLC_TIMEOUT` seconds per TLC run (5400),
`MODEL_SIMS` random witness traces per schedule (8). Generated TLC inputs go to `tmp/model-regen/<name>/` (never
committed); each run writes `observe/<run>.jsonl` (the counterexample if there is one, otherwise the shortest
behaviour that reaches the schedule's end) and `model-regen/results/schedules/<name>/` (verdict, TLC tails, traces,
the decision-replay report). `run.sh` resolves `testbed/schedules/<name>.yaml` and accepts any schedule in the format;
a schedule the format does not allow is reported `UNEXPLAINED rejected <reason>`.

One run of `run.sh <name>`:

2. TLC explores, breadth first and exhaustively within the bounds below, `SpecL` against every safety invariant
